stem: Which term best describes the actual shape of the earth?
options: A perfect sphere
An oblate spheroid
A prolate ellipsoid
A flat circular disc
explanation: Correct option: (B). The earth bulges at the equator and is slightly flattened at the poles, so it resembles an oblate spheroid. It is not a perfect sphere because the equatorial and polar radii differ; a prolate ellipsoid would be stretched at the poles, and a flat disc is an outdated idea.

stem: Which two natural points of reference on the earth form the basis of the geographical grid?
options: The equator and the Prime Meridian
The Tropic of Cancer and Tropic of Capricorn
The North Pole and the South Pole
Greenwich and the International Date Line
explanation: Correct option: (C). The spinning of the earth on its axis gives two natural reference points, the North and South Poles, on which the grid is built. The equator, tropics, Prime Meridian and Date Line are all lines drawn with reference to these poles; the Prime Meridian is chosen by agreement, not given by nature.

stem:
Assertion (A): The equatorial radius of the earth is greater than its polar radius.
Reason (R): The rotation of the earth on its axis produces a bulge at the equator.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
explanation: Correct option: (A). Both statements are true. The rotation of the earth causes bulging at the equator, which makes the equatorial radius larger than the polar radius. Hence R correctly explains A.

stem: Why are latitudes and longitudes together called geographical coordinates?
options: They show the height of places above sea level
They divide the earth into climatic and time zones only
They give the shape and size of every continent
They form a network that fixes the position of any point
explanation: Correct option: (D). Latitudes and longitudes form a systematic network of intersecting lines on which the location, distance and direction of points can be fixed, which is why they are coordinates. They do not measure height, they are not limited to zones, and they do not by themselves describe continental shapes.

stem: A student argues that without the grid there would be no way to state the exact position of a ship in mid-ocean. Which feature of the earth best supports this argument?
options: A spherical surface has no natural fixed starting point
The oceans cover more area than the continents
The earth revolves around the sun once a year
Ocean currents keep moving floating objects around
explanation: Correct option: (A). On a nearly spherical surface there is no natural point of reference from which to measure positions, so an imaginary grid of parallels and meridians is needed. Ocean area, revolution and currents do not explain why a reference network is required to state position.

stem: The latitude of a place is its angular distance measured
options: east or west of the Prime Meridian
north or south of the equator
from the International Date Line
from the Tropic of Cancer
explanation: Correct option: (B). Latitude is the angular distance of a point north or south of the equator, measured along the meridian of the place as an angle from the centre of the earth. Distance east or west of the Prime Meridian is longitude; the Date Line and the tropics are not reference lines for latitude.

stem: If parallels of latitude are drawn at an interval of one degree, how many parallels will there be in all, including the equator?
explanation: Correct option: (C). There are 89 parallels in each hemisphere (1 degree to 89 degrees; the poles at 90 degrees are points, not circles). Total = 89 + 89 + 1 (equator) = 179. 178 omits the equator, while 180 and 181 wrongly count the poles as lines.

stem: While drawing the parallel of 20 degrees S on a circle, where should the two points at 20 degrees from the equator be marked?
options: In the upper half of the circle, east and west
Along the vertical diameter of the circle
At the centre and on the circumference
In the lower half of the circle, east and west
explanation: Correct option: (D). With the equator as the horizontal diameter, southern latitudes lie in the lower half. Two points are marked at 20 degrees from the equator on the east and west sides of the lower half and joined by a line parallel to the equator. The upper half would give 20 degrees N; the other choices do not give a parallel.

stem:
Assertion (A): One degree of latitude near the poles is slightly longer than one degree of latitude at the equator.
Reason (R): The earth is not a perfect sphere but is flattened at the poles.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
explanation: Correct option: (A). Both are true. A degree of latitude is about 110.6 km at the equator and about 111.7 km at the poles. This happens because the earth is an oblate spheroid; if it were a perfect sphere, every degree of latitude would have the same length. So R explains A.

stem: The Prime Meridian, given the value of 0 degrees, passes through
options: Greenwich, near London
Mirzapur in India
Paris in France
the North Pole only
explanation: Correct option: (A). By international agreement the meridian passing through the Greenwich observatory near London was adopted as the Prime Meridian (0 degrees). stem: Which statement about meridians of longitude is correct?
options: They are full circles of decreasing size
They are parallel to the equator
They are equal semicircles meeting at the poles
They are farthest apart near the poles
explanation: Correct option: (C). Meridians are semicircles that converge at the poles and are all equal in length. Circles of decreasing size parallel to the equator describe parallels of latitude, and meridians are farthest apart at the equator, not at the poles.

stem: The distance between two adjacent meridians one degree apart is about 111.3 km at the equator. What is it at about 45 degrees of latitude?
options: 0 km
79 km
111 km
56 km
explanation: Correct option: (B). Meridians converge towards the poles, so the distance between them falls from about 111.3 km at the equator to 0 km at the poles; at 45 degrees it is about 79 km. 111 km is the equatorial value, 0 km is the polar value, and 56 km is simply half, which ignores how the distance actually changes.

stem: When meridians are drawn on a circle whose centre represents the North Pole, the 45 degrees E meridian appears on the drawer's left. Why?
options: East is always on the left on every map
The drawing is made of the southern hemisphere
Meridians run east-west in a polar view
Seen from above the North Pole, east and west reverse
explanation: Correct option: (D). When you imagine standing at the North Pole and look down at the earth, the usual directions reverse: east is on the left and west on the right. On an ordinary map east is on the right, the view is of the northern hemisphere, and meridians still run north-south.

stem: Which pair correctly contrasts parallels of latitude with meridians of longitude?
options: Parallels vary in length; meridians are equal
Parallels converge at poles; meridians do not
Parallels are semicircles; meridians are circles
Parallels range to 180 degrees; meridians to 90
explanation: Correct option: (A). Parallels get smaller from the equator to the poles, while all meridians are equal in length. It is meridians, not parallels, that converge at the poles; meridians are semicircles and parallels are circles; and latitude runs to 90 degrees while longitude runs to 180 degrees.

stem: How much time does the sun take to traverse one degree of longitude?
options: 1 minute
15 minutes
4 minutes
60 minutes
explanation: Correct option: (C). The earth rotates 360 degrees in 24 hours, that is 15 degrees per hour, so 1 degree takes 60/15 = 4 minutes. 15 minutes and 60 minutes confuse degrees with hourly rates, and 1 minute is far too short.

75 degrees E
90 degrees E
68 degrees 7 minutes E
explanation: Correct option: (A). IST is based on the 82 degrees 30 minutes E meridian passing through Mirzapur. 75 degrees and 90 degrees E are whole-hour meridians, and 68 degrees 7 minutes E is near India's western limit, not its standard meridian.

stem: When it is 12.00 noon at Greenwich, what is the local time at a place on 60 degrees W longitude?
explanation: Correct option: (B). Time difference = 60 x 4 = 240 minutes = 4 hours. Places west of Greenwich are behind it, so 12.00 noon - 4 hours = 8.00 a.m. 4.00 p.m. adds the time (that would be 60 degrees E); 10.00 a.m. and 4.00 a.m. use wrong differences.

stem:
Assertion (A): Indian Standard Time is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich Mean Time.
Reason (R): India's standard meridian, 82 degrees 30 minutes E, is a multiple of 7 degrees 30 minutes.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
explanation: Correct option: (B). A is true: 82.5 x 4 = 330 minutes = 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT. R is also true, since 82.5 = 11 x 7.5. But R only explains why the difference is a neat half-hour multiple; the actual 5 h 30 min comes from the meridian lying 82.5 degrees east of Greenwich. So R is not the correct explanation of A.

stem: When it is 10 a.m. at the Prime Meridian, it is 4 p.m. at place P and 5 a.m. at place Q. What are the longitudes of P and Q?
options: P 90 degrees W; Q 75 degrees E
P 60 degrees E; Q 50 degrees W
P 90 degrees E; Q 75 degrees W
P 75 degrees E; Q 90 degrees W
explanation: Correct option: (C). P is 6 hours ahead: 6 x 60 / 4 = 90 degrees, east because time is ahead, so 90 degrees E. Q is 5 hours behind: 5 x 15 = 75 degrees, west because time is behind, so 75 degrees W. The other options reverse the directions or use wrong conversions.

stem: The International Date Line runs approximately along which meridian?
options: 0 degrees
90 degrees E
82 degrees 30 minutes E
180 degrees
explanation: Correct option: (D). The International Date Line roughly follows the 180 degree meridian, exactly 12 hours from the Prime Meridian. 0 degrees is the Prime Meridian, 82 degrees 30 minutes E is India's standard meridian, and 90 degrees E has no date significance.

stem: The time at the 180 degree meridian differs from the time at 0 degrees longitude by
options: 6 hours
12 hours
24 hours
18 hours
explanation: Correct option: (B). 180 degrees x 4 minutes = 720 minutes = 12 hours, whether one goes east or west from the Prime Meridian. 24 hours is a full rotation, and 6 or 18 hours do not match 180 degrees.

stem: A traveller moving eastward crosses the International Date Line on a Tuesday. How should the day be counted after crossing?
options: As Monday
As Wednesday
As Tuesday still
As Thursday
explanation: Correct option: (A). Crossing the Date Line eastward, the traveller sets the calendar back by one day, so Tuesday becomes Monday. Wednesday would apply to a westward crossing, keeping Tuesday ignores the date change, and Thursday skips two days.

stem: Why is a date line needed at all once the world is divided into 24 time zones?
options: Time zones are not equal in width
Clocks run faster in the east
Going round the world gains or loses a day
The equator splits the earth in two
explanation: Correct option: (C). Moving east, a traveller keeps advancing clocks and moving west keeps setting them back; after a full circuit this adds up to a whole day. A date line at 180 degrees is where this day is corrected. Zone widths, the equator and clock speed are irrelevant.

stem:
Assertion (A): Two places just on either side of the International Date Line have nearly the same clock time but different dates.
Reason (R): The Date Line follows the 180 degree meridian, where the time is 12 hours ahead when reached going east and 12 hours behind when reached going west.
options: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
explanation: Correct option: (A). Both are true. Reached eastward the 180 degree meridian is 12 hours ahead of Greenwich, and reached westward it is 12 hours behind, a 24-hour gap. So places on either side share almost the same clock time but differ by one calendar day, which R explains.
